periods.analysis: At 18%, chronic absenteeism is above our <=15% target but still in yellow, which tells me the issue is serious and still movable. This quarter is our baseline for the new school year arc, and the pattern is clearest in grades 6, 9, and 10 at Bayfront Middle, Seaport High, and Eastgate K-8. Harborview’s growth is showing up in classrooms: new-to-district students, longer bus runs from the north waterfront, and families moving between temporary leases are all creating attendance friction. I am not satisfied with 18%, but I do see enough early signal in the daily dashboard to act before this becomes normalized.
periods.recommendations: Keep the citywide Attendance First protocol active and require every school to review its 10-day absence roster each Monday by student, not just by percentage. Add targeted family outreach on the Route 14 and Route 22 bus corridors, where late arrivals are converting into full-day absences. Sustain the school-based attendance liaisons at Bayfront, Seaport, and Eastgate, and extend text-message nudges to all grade 6 and grade 9 households by the next reporting cycle.

periods.analysis: Chronic absenteeism rose to 18.8%, up 0.8 points from 18%, so the yellow condition is getting heavier rather than lighter. The increase followed the expected holiday and respiratory-illness season, but the size of the movement tells us this is not just weather and flu. Our Student Support Office found repeat absences clustered among ninth graders at Seaport High and multilingual newcomer students at Harborview Central, especially where families missed re-enrollment or transportation updates. The watch-item is clear: if we let winter absence patterns set, spring recovery becomes much harder.
periods.recommendations: Direct principals to run two-week attendance sprints before and after winter break, with same-day calls on the second consecutive absence. Pair the health department’s school nurse team with attendance liaisons so illness-related absences trigger return-to-school planning instead of passive waiting. Extend multilingual attendance letters and robocalls in Spanish, Vietnamese, Arabic, and Haitian Creole for all schools with chronic absenteeism above 18.8%.

periods.analysis: The rate moved to 19.5%, up another 0.7 points from 18.8%, keeping us in yellow but now very close to the red line. I read this as a warning flare: the students are telling us that the barriers are becoming more durable than our current interventions. Winter bus reliability on the airport industrial loop, housing instability near the Westhaven shelter corridor, and disengagement among credit-deficient ninth graders are now overlapping. The one encouraging note is that schools using daily advisory check-ins, especially Northport Academy and Maritime CTE, held their increases smaller than the districtwide movement.
periods.recommendations: Stand up an Attendance Command Review for the 12 schools over 19.5%, chaired weekly by the chief of student support and including transportation, housing outreach, and school operations. Expand daily advisory check-ins from Northport Academy and Maritime CTE to the full ninth-grade cohort at Seaport, Harborview Central, and South Channel High. Set a concrete trigger: any school with a two-week increase of 0.3 points or more must submit a student-level recovery list within five school days.

periods.analysis: Chronic absenteeism reached 20.4%, up 0.9 points from 19.5%, and that moves the measure into red. This is the moment to be plain: too many students are missing too much school, and the trend is now outside acceptable operating range. The end-of-year audits show the sharpest movement among housing-insecure students, students with prior-year course failures, and elementary students on the Tideflats and North Marina bus routes. We have begun the Attendance Pipeline Renewal work, moving from generic reminders to a case-managed pipeline that identifies the student, the barrier, the responsible adult, and the closure date.
periods.recommendations: Implement Attendance Pipeline Renewal in all red-tier schools, beginning with the 1,200 students who crossed the 10% absence threshold before spring break. Assign each student a named case owner, with weekly barrier coding for transportation, health, housing, safety, or engagement. Use summer bridge enrollment, credit recovery, and family conferences as attendance re-entry tools so the next school year does not inherit the same roster of disconnected students.

periods.analysis: The rate increased to 21%, up 0.6 points from 20.4%, so we remain red, but the quarter-over-quarter rise slowed after the sharper spring jump. That slower movement matters, but I will not confuse deceleration with success. Early implementation of Attendance Pipeline Renewal produced better contact rates at Portside Elementary and Eastgate K-8, while Seaport High and South Channel High still show persistent non-attendance among students who entered the year already credit-deficient. The first 20 days of school confirmed that transportation and family mobility remain the two biggest operational barriers.
periods.recommendations: Keep Attendance Pipeline Renewal in place and require schools to close the loop on every student contacted, documenting whether the intervention actually restored attendance. Add morning arrival monitors and late-bus sweeps on the Tideflats, North Marina, and airport industrial routes for the first six weeks of the term. Concentrate mentoring slots on grades 6 and 9, because those transitions are where we can still prevent a full-year chronic pattern.

periods.analysis: Chronic absenteeism rose to 21.5%, up 0.5 points from 21%, which keeps us in red while showing a second quarter of slower growth. That is managed concern, not comfort. The Attendance Pipeline Renewal teams are now active in 18 schools, and their best results are coming where principals schedule home visits within 72 hours of a third absence in a month. The remaining pressure is concentrated in winter illness, family displacement from rising rents, and older students balancing school with paid work in the port and airport service economy.
periods.recommendations: Protect the 72-hour home-visit standard and add Saturday family conference blocks at Seaport High, Harborview Central, and South Channel High. Work with major airport and port employers to distribute school attendance expectations and youth work-hour guidance to families of employed students. Expand telehealth and nurse follow-up for repeat illness absences so medically fragile students can return safely and quickly.

periods.analysis: The rate reached 21.8%, up 0.3 points from 21.5%, so we are still red, but the pace of deterioration has slowed for the third consecutive quarter. I see that as evidence that the operating model is beginning to grip the problem, even though the level remains unacceptable. Pipeline Renewal case notes show fewer unreachable families, with contact completion improving at Bayfront Middle, Portside Elementary, and Harborview Central. The watch now is whether we can convert contact into sustained attendance, particularly for students with three or more barriers coded in the system.
periods.recommendations: Move the highest-need students into multidisciplinary attendance panels that include the principal, counselor, nurse, housing navigator, and transportation dispatcher. Require a four-week attendance contract for every student with three or more coded barriers, with a named adult checking in twice weekly. Sustain the improved family contact process, but add a persistence metric: students must show two consecutive weeks of improved attendance before a case is considered stabilized.

periods.analysis: Chronic absenteeism is now 22%, up 0.2 points from 21.8%, keeping the measure red while continuing the pattern of smaller quarterly increases. The city and schools have not turned the curve yet, but we have reduced the acceleration from the 0.9-point jump seen when the measure first crossed into red. Attendance Pipeline Renewal is giving us a cleaner operating picture: transportation barriers are concentrated on five route clusters, while housing-related absences remain highest around Westhaven, North Marina, and the downtown motel corridor. My judgment is that the system is more disciplined than it was a year ago, but students still need us to move from containment to reversal.
periods.recommendations: Set a next-quarter objective to stop growth entirely by holding chronic absenteeism at or below 22% while building toward the <=15% target over the longer recovery cycle. Rebid or adjust the five highest-absence bus route clusters before the opening month, including earlier pickup windows and backup vans for missed connections. Keep Pipeline Renewal active through summer, with case owners carrying students into summer learning, re-enrollment, and the first 30 days of the next school year rather than closing cases at the end of term.

periods.analysis: Chronic absenteeism increased from 22.0% to 22.1%, moving away from the 15% ceiling. The increase is small, but the promised reversal has not occurred.
periods.recommendations: Carry named attendance cases through the first school-year review and check whether transportation and housing barriers identified in the five route clusters have been resolved.
